query: Using the reported HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high-entropy alloy as the starting material and its quasi-static properties—786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% fracture strain—as the baseline, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to overcome limited strain hardening, poor uniform deformability, and rapid failure as strain rate increases under adiabatic dynamic deformation? Specify the intervention and mechanism, predict changes relative to the baseline in strength, uniform deformation, localization resistance, and impact-induced energy release, define the strain-rate and loading conditions over which the prediction applies, cite supporting evidence from the reported refractory-alloy literature, and describe a matched baseline-versus-intervention experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small interstitial oxygen content (~0.5–1 at.%) into the HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high‐entropy alloy will increase dynamic strain hardening, delay the onset of localization, and thus improve uniform deformability and energy absorption under adiabatic dynamic deformation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high‐entropy alloy with quasi‐static properties of 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% fracture strain, exhibiting a single-phase BCC structure.
generation.intervention: Interstitial doping with oxygen at a low atomic percentage (e.g., 0.5–1 at.% addition during alloy processing).
generation.conditions: Adiabatic dynamic deformation conditions at high strain rates (on the order of 10^3 s⁻¹) such as those achievable in split-Hopkinson pressure bar tests, where rapid plastic deformation and localized heating are significant.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased lattice distortion and modified short-range ordering due to interstitial oxygen occupying octahedral interstitial sites, which can act as pinning points for dislocations.
generation.mechanism: Oxygen atoms in interstitial sites induce additional lattice distortion that increases the energy barriers for dislocation motion. Under high strain rate conditions, this promotes enhanced dynamic strain hardening and delays the onset of shear localization (adiabatic shear banding), thereby improving uniform deformation and impact energy absorption.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the oxygen-doped variant is predicted to show an increase in dynamic yield and compressive strengths (by an uncertain but notable margin), a higher uniform plastic strain before failure, improved strain rate sensitivity (enhanced resistance to localization), and greater impact-induced energy absorption under rapid loading conditions.
generation.baseline: Quasi-static properties of the undoped HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy: 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% fracture strain.
generation.boundary: The improvements are predicted primarily under high strain rate, adiabatic dynamic deformation scenarios. Under quasi-static or lower strain rate conditions, the benefits of the oxygen addition may be less pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of strength and ductility improvements under dynamic conditions is uncertain due to limited direct data on interstitially doped refractory HEAs; the optimal oxygen content for balancing enhancement in strain hardening against potential embrittlement also requires fine-tuning.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy without oxygen addition and a second set with a controlled 0.5–1 at.% oxygen interstitial doping. Process the alloys under identical conditions to ensure similar grain structures and phases. Subject both sample sets to dynamic compression tests (e.g., using a split-Hopkinson pressure bar) at strain rates around 10^3 s⁻¹ under adiabatic conditions.
measurements: Dynamic yield strength and compressive strength
Uniform plastic strain prior to failure
Strain rate sensitivity and strain-hardening rate
Impact-induced energy absorption (by monitoring temperature rise/distribution and energy dissipation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in dynamic strength, enhanced strain-hardening (i.e., a higher uniform plastic strain before localization), and greater impact energy absorption compared to the baseline alloy under the specified high strain rate conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Effect of Al Content on Phase Structure and Microstructure of High-Entropy Alloys Figure 1 presents the X-ray diffraction patterns and the diffraction peaks of the (110) planes for the AlxCr0.2NbTiV alloys (x = 0.2, 0.5, or 0.8). As shown in Figure 1a, these alloys exhibit a BCC single-phase structure. With the increase in Al content, the intensity of the diffraction peaks at the (110) crystal planes progressively strengthens, and the peak positions shift noticeably towards larger angles, as shown in Figure 1b, with the lattice constant decreasing from 3.198 Å to 3.184 Å. Since Al is a formative element for the BCC structure, increasing the Al content enhances the stability of the BCC phase and hence the strengthening of the (110) diffraction peak [,]; moreover, although Al’s atomic radius is larger than that of Cr, it is similar to that of other elements in the alloy. Al enters the alloy via substitutional solid solution, leading to a decrease in the lattice constant, which causes the diffraction peaks to shift towards larger angles []. This study employed first-principles calculations combined with the Special Quasi-random Structure (SQS) technique to systematically investigate the effects of interstitial elements C, N, and O on the structural, electronic, and mechanical properties of NiCoCr medium-entropy alloys (MEAs). The key findings are summarized as follows: Interstitial site preference and lattice distortion: C and N preferentially occupy octahedral interstitial sites, while O exhibits a higher diffusion rate between octahedral and tetrahedral sites, effectively alleviating stress concentration. The dissolution of these interstitial atoms causes significant lattice distortion, with O causing the most noticeable distortion (16.82%), followed by N (10.84%) and C (9.27%). Mechanical properties: The introduction of interstitial atoms increases the elastic constants and SFE, indicating an improvement in stiffness and resistance to plastic deformation. O doping leads to the most significant increase in SFE (69 mJ/m2, from −35 mJ/m2 to 34 mJ/m2), followed by N (58 mJ/m2) and C (54 mJ/m2).
